newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Candle vigil crowns anti-Japan protests in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Candle vigil crowns anti-Japan protests in Hong Kong.

text.p: Thousands of Hong Kong Chinese waved candles and shouted "down with Japanese militarism" as a wave of anti-Japan protests over Tokyo's claim to a group of disputed islands hit a new high in Hong Kong on Wednesday.
A flurry of rallies, scuffles and candlelight vigils marked the day, the 65th anniversary of Japan's invasion of China.
Britain called for calm in its colony, saying things could run of control unless passions were dampened.
But evening drizzle failed to dampen the enthusiasm of the up to 8,000 people who ignored the rain to join a candlelight rally on Hong Kong's Tsim Sha Tsui peninsula.

Pro-Taiwan Chinese Nationalist veterans took centre stage for a while, waving Taiwan flags and drawing loud applause from the candle-waving throng seated on the concrete ground against the backdrop of Hong Kong harbour's high-rise skyline.

September 18 is a painful date in the Chinese memory because the invasion of northeast China marked the start of a 14-year military carve-up by Japanese forces, accompanied by a string of war atrocities against millions of Chinese civilians.
Hong Kong, a British colony due to revert to China next July 1, was occupied by Japan from 1941 to 1945.

Anti-Japan protests have grown steadily over the past month, sparked by Japan's renewed claim to the East China Sea islands that China calls the Diaoyus and known in Japan as the Senkakus. Both countries claim the islands have been theirs for centuries.

The protesters, including entire families, sang anti-Japanese war songs and waved banners with the slogans "Down with Japanese militarism", "The blood of the Sino-Japanese war is not dry", "Educate the next generation" and "Defend the Diaoyu Islands".
"The Diaoyu Islands belong to the Chinese people. I don't care which government it is, I only know the islands belong to China," housewife Chan Mee-chun, 49, told Reuters.

An elderly Taiwan veteran wearing a Nationalist Kuomintang cap and flak jacket who fought Japan as a soldier in the army of the pre-communist Kuomintang government, said the islands should belong to Taiwan, the Nationalists' last refuge.

"Thousands of people have turned out to urge the Chinese government to take action to recover the islands. We urge the Japanese government to withdraw," said Democratic Party legislator Cheung Man-kwong, one of the rally organisers.
"All Asian people unite against Japanese militarism," chanted the crowd. At one point they observed a minute's silence for the victims of the war, standing with their candles raised high.

Earlier there were violent scuffles in a Japanese department store in the prime shopping district of Causeway Bay as protesters shouting for a boycott of Japanese goods invaded the shop and clashed with workers and security guards.
Youths launched an overnight sit-down protest in the Exchange Square financial hub of Hong Kongs's main business quarter.
Ships blew their horns at noon in harmony with the protests.
Elderly men who survived the war gathered in the town of Sai Kung in the rural New Terriories to remember fallen comrades.
A succession of protest groups dumped petitions -- up to 760,000 Hong Kong people have signed -- at the door of the Japanese consulate.
Senior Trade Commissioner Francis Cornish, London's top diplomat in Hong Kong, called for cool heads to avoid trouble.
"All of us understand that this is an issue that does arouse strong feelings. These feelings should be expressed with restraint," Cornish said in an interview on government radio.
Japan has claimed sovereign rights to the islands and has refused to acknowledge the dispute is open for discussion.
Tokyo's claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has also claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
